claims.text: Nanoscale phase separation governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
The relevant phase-separated structure consists of finely distributed ferromagnetic clusters embedded in a paramagnetic matrix.
This heterogeneous nanostructure facilitates rapid magnetic-domain reorientation under low applied fields.
The heterogeneous nanostructure minimizes magnetic hysteresis losses.
The phase-separated nanostructure retains mechanical coherence.
Controlled heat treatment or aging can induce and tune nanoscale phase separation.
The proposed heat treatment can form a bimodal distribution of ferromagnetic clusters and a paramagnetic matrix.
The useful phase-separation regime lies below the alloy's homogenization temperature and above the temperature at which detrimental coarsening occurs.
Nanoscale phase-separated regions modify magnetic-domain behavior.
Nanoscale phase-separated regions modify thermal-transport pathways.
Nanostructural heterogeneity enhances low-field magnetocaloric response through sensitive and cooperative nucleation and growth of ferromagnetic domains.
The increased interfacial area of the fine phase dispersion improves the rate of heat exchange.
A mechanically coherent matrix reduces hysteresis and preserves overall alloy stability.
Relative to the untreated homogeneous baseline, the heat-treated alloy will have a larger low-field magnetocaloric effect and increased isothermal entropy change.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit reduced magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the heat-treated alloy will maintain or improve its mechanical properties.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit faster thermal response times.
The hypothesis applies near room temperature only where nanoscale phase separation is thermodynamically feasible without large-scale phase deterioration.
